title: Aurora Financial — SSO / SCIM + Audit Logs Export Review
summary: Aurora Financial walked through their baseline controls for vendor onboarding (SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, RBAC, audit logging to SIEM, and retention/deletion expectations). Redwood confirmed current SSO (SAML 2.0) coverage for Console, SCIM support scope (user provisioning + deprovisioning) and RBAC model at a high level, and the audit log event types + export options (download/API and export destinations depending on plan/deployment). Aurora’s key requirement is near-real-time audit log export into their SIEM (Splunk, with an S3 ingestion path also acceptable) and clarity on retention defaults for request logs vs audit logs. Redwood agreed to send the canonical docs (SSO/SCIM/RBAC capabilities page, audit logging customer overview, retention/deletion overview, and the SOC 2 evidence request process) and to confirm the most accurate wording for ‘real-time export’ and retention controls for their intended deployment (Dedicated vs Private).
topics: SAML SSO (IdP support, enforced SSO, break-glass access)
RBAC granularity in Console vs API
Audit log taxonomy and fields (auth, admin actions, key management, exports)
Audit log export options (SIEM/S3/HTTP) and delivery frequency
Retention: prompts/outputs, operational logs, audit logs; deletion timelines
Evidence requests: SOC 2 report under NDA and standard process
questions: Do you support SAML SSO for the admin console, and can you enforce it org-wide?
Do you support SCIM for automated provisioning and deprovisioning? Any group-to-role mapping?
What RBAC roles exist and can we restrict API key creation and model access?
What exactly is in the audit log, and can we export it to Splunk/SIEM in near real time?
What are the default retention periods for audit logs and any request logs? Can we set them to 0 or 7 days?
Do you store prompts/outputs, and do you train on customer data?
action_items: Markus Klein (Redwood) — Send Aurora the SSO/SAML/SCIM + RBAC capabilities doc and RBAC summary; include note on Console vs API coverage — Due 2026-02-21
Kevin Osei (Redwood) — Confirm current audit log export mechanisms and the approved wording for delivery frequency/latency; share the audit logging overview doc — Due 2026-02-21

Naomi Feldman (Redwood) — Validate retention/deletion wording for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (including ‘no training’ phrasing) and provide the approved snippet for Aurora questionnaire — Due 2026-02-24
Tom Nguyen (Aurora) — Share SIEM preferred ingestion method (Splunk HEC vs S3-based ingestion) and required fields list — Due 2026-02-24
Elena Petrova (Aurora) — Confirm NDA path/contact for requesting SOC 2 report and whether their procurement portal requires upload — Due 2026-02-25
next_steps: Redwood to email doc bundle: SSO/SCIM/RBAC capabilities + audit logging overview + retention/deletion overview + SOC 2 evidence request playbook.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up to map Aurora’s required audit events/fields to Redwood’s audit log taxonomy and confirm export path for their chosen deployment.
Aurora to confirm target deployment mode (Dedicated vs Private) and region requirements so Redwood can align the retention/export claims appropriately.
transcript:
Meeting: Aurora Financial — SSO / SCIM + Audit Logs Export Review
Recorded by Fireflies
Date: 2026-02-20
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Avery Johnson, Markus Klein, Kevin Osei, Naomi Feldman
Aurora Financial: Priya Desai, Tom Nguyen, Elena Petrova, Matt Rivera

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Aurora is validating Redwood controls for IAM, audit logging, and retention before moving forward with a Dedicated/Private evaluation.
- Key requirements: enforce SAML SSO for Console, automated user lifecycle (SCIM), RBAC separation of duties, exportable audit logs into Splunk (S3 acceptable), and clear retention/deletion story.
- Redwood will send canonical docs + confirm approved language for export frequency and retention defaults.


[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, hi everyone. Thanks for making time. This is Avery from Redwood. I’ve got Markus with me, Kevin from Security Engineering, and Naomi our product security PM.

[00:10] Priya Desai: Hi, Priya here. Tom is on, Elena from compliance, and Matt from platform.

[00:16] Markus Klein: Hey all.

[00:18] Kevin Osei: Hi.

[00:19] Naomi Feldman: Hello.

[00:22] Avery Johnson: Cool. Goal today is pretty narrow: SSO and provisioning, RBAC, and then audit logs export to SIEM plus retention. We’ll keep it tight and then we’ll send the doc pack after.

[00:35] Tom Nguyen: Yep, that’s what we need. We’re trying to avoid a long generic security overview and just get to the stuff our onboarding checklist calls out.

[00:45] Elena Petrova: And we’ll need the SOC report under NDA later, but today it’s more capabilities.

[00:51] Avery Johnson: Great. Priya do you want to start with SSO/SCIM requirements?

[00:56] Priya Desai: Sure. For any SaaS or console, we require SAML SSO, ideally with Okta. Enforced SSO, not “optional”. We also need SCIM so that when someone leaves, they’re deprovisioned automatically. And we generally want group-based access, like Okta group maps to roles.

[01:18] Priya Desai: Also we need to understand if there’s any local password login as a bypass and if that can be disabled. And for break-glass, we need a controlled approach.

[01:30] Markus Klein: Makes sense. On the Redwood side: for the Redwood Console, we support SAML 2.0 SSO with common IdPs, Okta is definitely a common one. Enforcing SSO org-wide is supported, meaning you can require users authenticate via the IdP.

[01:49] Priya Desai: So no username/password at all?

[01:53] Markus Klein: There is an admin configuration where you can require SSO. There are still “break glass” patterns, but we handle those as tightly controlled admin accounts. Kevin, do you want to add how we talk about break-glass?

[02:06] Kevin Osei: Yeah. Generally, we don’t position it as “backdoor”. It’s more like: you can maintain a limited number of emergency admin accounts that are excluded from SSO enforcement for continuity, but those are monitored and protected. In practice, most customers keep it to one or two accounts, stored in a password vault with strong MFA.

[02:25] Tom Nguyen: And the activity on those accounts would show in audit logs, right?

[02:28] Kevin Osei: Yes, admin actions and auth events are part of the audit log taxonomy. We can send the exact event list we publish.

[02:36] Priya Desai: Ok. SCIM—do you do full SCIM or partial?

[02:41] Markus Klein: SCIM provisioning and deprovisioning is supported for Console users. Group mapping is… Naomi, can you help me phrase this precisely? I don’t want to overstate.

[02:53] Naomi Feldman: Yeah. The safe framing is: SCIM supports automated user lifecycle (create, deactivate) and basic attribute sync. For group-to-role mapping, we support role assignment in the Console and via admin workflows; some customers do this through group conventions, but the exact “dynamic group mapping” behavior depends on configuration and is not something we should promise as fully automatic unless we confirm the specific setup.

[03:20] Priya Desai: So if we have an Okta group “Redwood-ReadOnly”, can that automatically assign a read-only role?

[03:28] Markus Klein: We should validate the current behavior for your exact ask. We can usually meet the intent: least privilege and automated deprovisioning, and then role assignment can be managed by admins or via supported mapping. Let me confirm and come back with the approved statement.

[03:45] Priya Desai: Got it. As long as deprovision is solid. That’s a hard requirement.

[03:52] Markus Klein: Yep.

[03:54] Matt Rivera: Quick one—does SSO cover API usage or just console?

[04:00] Markus Klein: Great question. The SAML SSO is for Console interactive access. For API access, you typically use API keys or service accounts. The control is in RBAC and key management: who can create keys, rotate them, restrict scopes.

[04:15] Tom Nguyen: That’s the next topic—RBAC. We need separation of duties. For example, a developer shouldn’t be able to create org-wide keys and also change audit log exports.

[04:26] Avery Johnson: Makes sense. Kevin, do you want to outline the RBAC model at a high level?

[04:31] Kevin Osei: Sure. Redwood provides organization-level roles that control access in the Console and admin APIs. Typical roles include admin and read-only, plus scoped roles for billing/usage and operational settings. The key thing is: permissions cover sensitive actions like managing members, configuring auth, creating and managing API keys, and viewing/exporting logs.

[04:55] Kevin Osei: We also support limiting who can access certain projects or endpoints depending on your setup, especially in Dedicated/Private deployments where you can align it to your internal tenancy model.

[05:07] Priya Desai: Are there custom roles or is it fixed roles?

[05:11] Kevin Osei: It’s primarily a defined set of roles today, with some granularity around permissions. We have an internal RBAC capabilities summary we can share that’s meant for RFPs—what roles exist and what they can do.

[05:25] Tom Nguyen: That’s fine, we just need it documented.

[05:28] Avery Johnson: We’ll include that in the send list.

[05:31] Elena Petrova: I’m going to jump a bit ahead—do you have SSO + SCIM included by default or is it an enterprise add-on?

[05:39] Avery Johnson: For enterprise accounts it’s generally included; exact packaging depends on plan and deployment mode. We’ll follow up with what your commercial proposal includes, but technically, yes, these capabilities are supported.

[05:55] Elena Petrova: Okay.

[05:57] Avery Johnson: Let’s move to audit logging since that’s the big one. Tom, can you lay out your requirement?

[06:04] Tom Nguyen: Sure. We need an audit trail of administrative actions. Specifically: logins, SSO events, user adds/removes, key creation/rotation, role changes, policy changes, model config changes, and any export configuration changes. We also need a way to ship those logs to our SIEM. We use Splunk. We can ingest from S3 or via HEC endpoint.

[06:28] Tom Nguyen: We also care about delivery time. It doesn’t have to be instantaneous, but we can’t have “here’s a CSV once a week”. We need near-real-time or at least frequent, like every few minutes or hourly.

[06:43] Matt Rivera: And format wise, JSON is best.

[06:46] Markus Klein: Totally. Redwood’s audit logs are structured events (JSON) with event type, timestamp, actor, target resource, and metadata fields. There are viewing and download options in Console, and for enterprise deployments we support exporting the audit logs.

[07:08] Tom Nguyen: Exporting how?

[07:10] Kevin Osei: There are a couple patterns. One is delivery to customer-controlled object storage—most commonly an S3 bucket in your account. Another is export via API or a push to an HTTPS endpoint depending on configuration. The exact options can vary by deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) and your security posture.

[07:32] Tom Nguyen: So you do support S3 delivery.

[07:35] Kevin Osei: Yes, that’s a common integration. We should confirm the details for your target deployment so we can give you the right language (frequency, guarantees, etc.).

[07:47] Priya Desai: For Private, would it run inside our VPC and then we can just forward logs internally?

[07:53] Markus Klein: In Private deployments, you have more control because the components are inside your network boundary, so integrating with your logging pipeline is usually straightforward. But we still want to align on the exact architecture you’re considering.

[08:07] Tom Nguyen: Our preference is Dedicated first, then possibly Private if the regulators push.

[08:12] Avery Johnson: Got it.

[08:14] Elena Petrova: Can you list what’s included in audit logs versus operational logs? We’ve had vendors say “audit logs” but it’s really app logs.

[08:23] Kevin Osei: Good distinction. Audit logs are security-relevant “who did what” actions: auth events, admin settings, user management, key management, org configuration, export configuration, etc. Operational logs are more like service-level metrics and debugging information.

[08:42] Kevin Osei: For inference content specifically (prompts/outputs), that’s not treated as audit logging. That falls under request logging / telemetry and has separate retention controls.

[08:53] Tom Nguyen: Okay, that’s exactly the next question—do you log prompts and outputs, and how long do you keep them?

[08:59] Naomi Feldman: I can take that. Redwood’s policy is: we do not train foundation models on customer prompts/outputs by default. For service operation, there can be limited logging for abuse prevention and troubleshooting, but retention is bounded and configurable depending on deployment mode and plan.

[09:18] Naomi Feldman: We’ll share the customer-facing retention/deletion overview, which breaks down: (1) customer content, (2) metadata/usage, (3) audit logs, and (4) support artifacts.

[09:31] Elena Petrova: Sorry to be direct—can we set retention to zero?

[09:35] Naomi Feldman: For some enterprise configurations, we can support “no content retention” beyond what’s required to process the request. However, there are always some minimal operational records (like billing/usage metadata) that are retained for compliance and invoicing. We should confirm your exact requirement, because “zero” can mean different things: zero prompt retention vs zero metadata vs zero audit log retention.

[09:59] Tom Nguyen: For us, the big thing is: no prompts/outputs stored. Audit logs we want to keep for at least a year in our SIEM.

[10:08] Naomi Feldman: That’s a common pattern: minimal/no content retention, but export audit logs to your SIEM where you keep them longer under your own controls.

[10:18] Matt Rivera: What’s the default retention on your side for audit logs?

[10:22] Kevin Osei: Default depends on plan; we generally have a standard retention window in product, and extended retention is available for enterprise/compliance packages. But because we want to avoid giving you a number that’s not aligned with your proposal, we’ll send the canonical statement and the options.

[10:40] Tom Nguyen: Understood. For the SIEM integration, do you have Splunk HEC “out of the box”?

[10:46] Kevin Osei: We have examples for SIEM integrations and a standard export format. Many Splunk pipelines accept S3 or HTTPS ingestion. We can provide guidance, but I don’t want to claim a single-click Splunk connector unless it’s actually in your environment. The core capability is: export the audit events in JSON to a destination you control.

[11:10] Tom Nguyen: Fair. But the frequency: can we do every five minutes?

[11:14] Markus Klein: The right wording is typically “near real-time” or “frequent export,” but we should confirm what the system supports today and what the SLA language is. Kevin will confirm and we’ll give you the approved phrasing for your questionnaire.

[11:30] Priya Desai: Also, do you have MFA?

[11:33] Markus Klein: When you use SSO, MFA is enforced at your IdP, so yes, effectively you can require MFA through Okta policies. For non-SSO break-glass accounts, you can require strong auth, but again we’ll share the recommended setup.

[11:50] Elena Petrova: And session timeout policies?

[11:53] Markus Klein: Session duration is configurable within bounds; exact details we’ll point to in the SSO/RBAC doc.

[12:05] Tom Nguyen: Another thing we need is audit log fields. We need actor IP, user agent, and request id correlation if possible.

[12:13] Kevin Osei: Some events include IP and user agent for Console access, and request identifiers for correlating actions. Not every event has every field, but we can share the event schema. There’s a doc that enumerates the audit log event taxonomy and typical fields.

[12:33] Matt Rivera: When you say “export via API,” is that like pulling with pagination?

[12:38] Kevin Osei: Yes, think of it as a programmatic retrieval for the audit log entries. And then the other mode is push to storage / endpoint.

[12:49] Priya Desai: For Dedicated, do we get a separate tenant for SSO and audit logs? Like isolation.

[12:55] Markus Klein: Dedicated is isolated capacity and data isolation at the infrastructure level; you have your own dedicated GPU pools. From the identity standpoint, it’s still a Redwood-managed control plane but with enterprise controls. Private is where you can move more of the control plane into your network boundary.

[13:18] Tom Nguyen: Right, that matches what we heard earlier.

[13:22] Avery Johnson: Let me pause and make sure we’re tracking: you need (1) SAML SSO enforced, (2) SCIM for deprovisioning, (3) RBAC roles documented, (4) audit log export to SIEM (Splunk via S3/HTTP), and (5) retention clarity for prompts/outputs and audit logs. That correct?

[13:40] Tom Nguyen: Yes.

[13:41] Priya Desai: Yes.

[13:42] Elena Petrova: Yes.

[13:45] Avery Johnson: Great. On retention, do you have a specific number? Like 7 days or 0?

[13:51] Elena Petrova: “No storage of customer content” is the key. If there’s any temporary retention for troubleshooting, we need it documented and ideally opt-out.

[14:03] Naomi Feldman: That’s exactly why we have the retention overview doc; it’s written to avoid ambiguous language. It breaks down what is stored, for what purpose, and how deletion works.

[14:16] Tom Nguyen: Deletion—if we offboard, can we request deletion of everything?

[14:21] Naomi Feldman: Yes, offboarding includes deletion workflows for customer data within the platform, subject to legal/contractual requirements for certain records like invoices. For Private deployments, you also control the underlying storage. Again, we’ll send the canonical wording.

[14:40] Priya Desai: Another detail: do you support SCIM deactivation events from Okta, and how fast does it take?

[14:47] Markus Klein: SCIM deprovisioning is designed to be near-immediate, but the exact propagation timing can vary. We should avoid committing to a hard number in a call; we’ll provide the supported behavior and any SLA if applicable.

[15:06] Priya Desai: Okay.

[15:08] Tom Nguyen: Can we talk about “shared responsibility”? Like, who does what in Dedicated vs Private.

[15:14] Avery Johnson: We can, but maybe just briefly since we’re timeboxed.

[15:18] Kevin Osei: In Hosted and Dedicated, Redwood operates the service, the runtime, and the underlying infra, and you control your org configuration, identity provider policies, and how you use API keys and integrate exports. In Private, responsibilities shift: you operate more of the environment (networking, certain patching/monitoring depending on the model), while Redwood provides the package and support. The one-pagers and security overview doc lay that out.

[15:49] Elena Petrova: For compliance, are you SOC 2? I’m assuming yes but we need a current report.

[15:56] Kevin Osei: We have a SOC 2 report that we share under NDA through an evidence request process. We’ll send the playbook link. We can’t email the report directly without the NDA and tracking.

[16:10] Elena Petrova: That’s fine.

[16:12] Tom Nguyen: ISO 27001—are you certified?

[16:16] Naomi Feldman: We’re careful with ISO language. We can discuss alignment and our control posture, but we won’t claim certification unless it’s current and in scope. The evidence process will cover what we can provide.

[16:32] Tom Nguyen: Okay, thanks for being direct.

[16:35] Matt Rivera: Audit log export: do you support customer-managed keys for encryption? Like KMS.

[16:41] Markus Klein: For Dedicated and Private we have options around customer-managed encryption keys depending on configuration. We’ll include the encryption/KMS one-pager in the follow-up if helpful, but today we can keep it to audit logs.

[16:55] Matt Rivera: If you’re delivering logs to our S3, we’d require SSE-KMS with our key.

[17:01] Kevin Osei: That’s a standard requirement. We can align on the specifics once we confirm the export architecture, but yes, delivering to your bucket with your encryption policy is something we see often.

[17:19] Tom Nguyen: Great.

[17:21] Avery Johnson: We have about 25 minutes left. Anything else on IAM?

[17:26] Priya Desai: Just one: do you have service accounts with non-human ownership?

[17:31] Markus Klein: Yes, we support non-human API access patterns (service accounts / API keys). The governance is: restricting key creation to admins, rotation, and monitoring via audit logs.

[17:48] Tom Nguyen: That would show in audit logs—key created, rotated, revoked.

[17:52] Kevin Osei: Correct.

[17:55] Elena Petrova: For retention, I’ll need your written policy that says you don’t use customer data to train.

[18:02] Naomi Feldman: We have an approved FAQ section and RFP language for “data use and training.” We’ll include that in the response pack.

[18:14] Tom Nguyen: Can you also clarify about subprocessors? We’ll ask later but just a heads-up.

[18:20] Avery Johnson: Yep, we have a standard subprocessor list and DPA process. We can route that through legal when you’re ready.

[18:28] Tom Nguyen: Okay.

[18:30] Avery Johnson: Let’s drill into audit events. Tom, you listed a set—login, user management, key actions, config changes. Anything else?

[18:39] Tom Nguyen: Access to logs themselves. Like “who viewed audit logs” should be auditable.

[18:44] Kevin Osei: Yep, log access events are included in the taxonomy.

[18:49] Tom Nguyen: And export configuration changes.

[18:52] Kevin Osei: Yes.

[18:54] Priya Desai: And SSO config changes.

[18:57] Kevin Osei: Yes.

[19:00] Matt Rivera: Any events around model deployments? Like switching model versions.

[19:06] Markus Klein: In deployment and rollout features, we have change events for configuration updates. The exact event types depend on what features you’re using (canaries, fallback policies, etc.). We can provide the list that applies.

[19:23] Tom Nguyen: Good.

[19:25] Avery Johnson: On export: you said Splunk. If S3 is acceptable, would you prefer that?

[19:31] Tom Nguyen: Probably S3 because we already have ingestion from S3 into Splunk. HEC is fine too. But we need to avoid an agent running on someone’s laptop, you know.

[19:41] Markus Klein: Understood.

[19:44] Kevin Osei: And to reiterate: we’ll confirm delivery cadence. Some exports are continuous-ish, some are scheduled intervals. We want to provide accurate language.

[19:57] Tom Nguyen: Perfect.

[20:00] Elena Petrova: On retention, do you distinguish between audit logs and “application logs”? Some vendors keep debug logs forever.

[20:08] Naomi Feldman: Yes, we separate categories. Audit logs have a defined retention in product; extended retention can be purchased. Operational logs are retained for limited periods for reliability and security monitoring, and they’re access-controlled. Customer content retention is separate and can be minimized.

[20:29] Elena Petrova: Okay.

[20:31] Priya Desai: We also require that vendors can provide evidence of access reviews. Is that something you can speak to?

[20:39] Kevin Osei: That’s part of our security program and is covered in SOC 2 controls. The evidence is in the SOC report and supporting artifacts we can share under NDA.

[20:52] Priya Desai: Fine.

[20:54] Avery Johnson: Quick check: any region/data residency requirements? I know Aurora is US-based but sometimes there are constraints.

[21:02] Elena Petrova: For this project it’s US-only. But we do have some data that can’t leave the US.

[21:08] Markus Klein: Okay, we can align to US regions for Hosted/Dedicated and discuss Private if needed.

[21:17] Tom Nguyen: Great.

[21:19] Avery Johnson: I want to be mindful of time. Let’s do a short “what we’ll send” list and then close.

[21:26] Markus Klein: Before we do, can I ask: are you evaluating other providers? Just so we know what comparisons you’re making.

[21:32] Tom Nguyen: We’ve looked at Bedrock and Azure OpenAI, and we have some internal stuff. But the reason we’re talking to you is Dedicated capacity + better controls.

[21:44] Avery Johnson: Got it.

[21:46] Naomi Feldman: And just to set expectation: if your questionnaire asks for something we don’t support as written, we have an exceptions policy and approved alternative language rather than ad-hoc answers.

[21:58] Elena Petrova: That’s good. We get annoyed when sales people improvise.

[22:02] Avery Johnson: Same.

[22:05] Avery Johnson: Alright—doc send list. We’ll send: (1) SSO/SAML/SCIM and RBAC capabilities doc, (2) an RBAC roles/permissions summary, (3) audit logging overview with event taxonomy and export options, (4) retention and deletion overview for customer-facing language, and (5) evidence request playbook for SOC 2 under NDA.

[22:28] Markus Klein: And we’ll include notes on Console vs API coverage.

[22:31] Kevin Osei: And I’ll follow up with the approved wording for “audit log export cadence” and what we can commit to.

[22:39] Naomi Feldman: I’ll provide the approved “data use / no training” snippet so it matches our FAQ.

[22:46] Tom Nguyen: Perfect.

[22:48] Priya Desai: Can you also include your supported IdPs list?

[22:52] Markus Klein: Yep, that’s in the SSO doc.

[22:56] Elena Petrova: One more: we need to know who to contact for evidence request turnaround times.

[23:01] Avery Johnson: The playbook has that and the SLA, and I’ll be the point person to coordinate.

[23:07] Tom Nguyen: Great.

[23:09] Avery Johnson: Next steps: we’ll send docs by tomorrow. Then let’s schedule a 30-min follow-up next week to map your required audit fields and confirm export method (S3 vs HTTPS). Does Tuesday work?

[23:22] Tom Nguyen: Tuesday afternoon works.

[23:24] Priya Desai: Works for me.

[23:26] Elena Petrova: I can join or just review notes.

[23:30] Avery Johnson: We’ll send notes.

[23:33] Matt Rivera: I’ll send you the list of required fields for SIEM ingestion.

[23:37] Kevin Osei: Perfect.

[23:40] Avery Johnson: Anything else before we wrap?

[23:43] Tom Nguyen: No, this was good. Thanks.

[23:46] Avery Johnson: Thanks everyone.

[23:48] Meeting ended.
